articles.title: Anglo-Saxons got special treatment in medieval Rome
articles.summary: A small hoard of medieval English coins found near the Vatican in Rome suggests that early English residents held a privileged status in the holy city
articles.content:
A small hoard of medieval English coins found near the Vatican in Rome suggests that early English residents held a privileged status in the holy city

Two fused groups of Anglo-Saxon coins found in the Palazzo della Rovere in Rome Cecilia de Leone

A rare collection of early-medieval coins found by archaeologists in Rome has provided a window into a time when English travellers and expats had special rights in the papal city and thrived in their own vibrant Anglo-Saxon quarter.

Historical records show that the English had their own area within the city, known as the Schola Saxonum. The newly uncovered hoard of coins, along with the remains of craft items such as leather, bone and metal, is the first material proof that the Anglo-Saxon quarter truly existed.

It also suggests that the English, unlike other foreign nationals, had the right to use their own currency in parts of Rome.

Advertisement

“The English quarter in Rome really was an interesting and vibrant place,” says Rory Naismith at the University of Cambridge. “It might be compared with districts in modern major cities that house a specific community, like the Chinatown areas of London, Melbourne, San Francisco and other cities.”

Since 2020, researchers have been excavating the walled garden of the Palazzo della Rovere near the Vatican, where they discovered the ruins of Emperor Nero’s theatre in 2023.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

The site has yielded a total of 30 coins, 23 of which were minted in the 10th century, including 20 Anglo-Saxon pennies and one half-penny of the early to mid-10th century, minted in the names of Edward the Elder (899–924), Æthelstan (924–39) and Eadred (946–55).

Along with the English currency, the archaeologists also found two Italian coins from the same era, along with six Roman or late antique bronze coins, as well as one unidentifiable bronze coin that may also be Roman.

Many of the coins have been fused together and are difficult to identify. Those that can still be read include specimens from several different parts of England: East Anglia, Kent, London and the West Midlands. Naismith and his colleagues have published their findings in a book, Rome and the Others (300-1000): Foreigners in the city between conflicts and integration.

Francesca Tinti at the University of the Basque Country, another member of the team, says the “shape, size and thickness” of the fused, unidentifiable coins are consistent with the clearly English ones. The non-English coins were found intermingled with the Anglo-Saxon currency, says Tinti.

“This seems to have been quite a busy, active area of the city, as the craft remains indicate,” she says.

Naismith says it is exceptional that most of these coins are English. Although many other English coins from the 10th century have been found in Rome, they have usually been regarded as religious donations, not as part of the regular currency of the city.

It was previously thought that the papacy banned the use of foreign currencies in Rome, but the new finds suggest that in this part of the city, English coins were used as a major part of the local currency, alongside local Italian coins.

“This is highly unusual for the 10th century – the norm was to use the local coin of whatever jurisdiction you were in,” Naismith says.

An account by the Welsh scholar Asser in 893 notes that Pope Marinus I had granted the English special rights in the 9th century in recognition of their demonstrations of piety.

Until now there has been no real archaeological evidence for what the Schola looked like, how it operated, or what privileges this community enjoyed, says Naismith.

He and Tinti had dreamed of finding piles of English coins and artefacts at the site in Rome, but never expected that their imagined finds would be more or less right, Naismith says.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a medieval Anglo-Saxon coin hoard in Rome provides significant archaeological evidence of historical cultural integration and special privileges granted to English residents in the papal city. This finding enriches understanding of medieval history and cross-cultural interactions, offering meaningful insights with broad historical and educational value.
articles.personality_title: Medieval English coins reveal special status in Rome
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Archaeologists have long known from old writings that English people living in medieval Rome had their own neighborhood called the Schola Saxonum. This area was believed to be a place where English travelers and residents lived and worked with some special rights.

**What happened** – Recently, a group of medieval English coins was found near the Vatican at the Palazzo della Rovere. The coins date back to the 10th century and come from different parts of England. Alongside these coins, remains of crafts like leather and metal were discovered. This is the first physical proof that the English quarter actually existed and that English coins were used there.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows that English residents in Rome were allowed to use their own money, which was unusual at the time. Normally, only local coins were accepted. The find also gives new details about the life and activity in the English quarter, proving it was a busy and special community within the city.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue studying the coins and artifacts to learn more about how the English community lived and worked in Rome. They hope to understand better the relationship between the English residents and the papal authorities, and how this special status affected trade and daily life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A rare hoard of Anglo-Saxon coins in Rome confirms that medieval English residents had unique privileges and a vibrant community in the heart of the papal city.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des pièces anglaises médiévales révèlent un statut spécial à Rome
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les historiens savaient grâce à des écrits anciens que des Anglais vivaient dans un quartier appelé Schola Saxonum à Rome au Moyen Âge. Ce lieu était un espace où les voyageurs et résidents anglais avaient des droits particuliers.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Récemment, un petit trésor de pièces anglaises médiévales a été découvert près du Vatican, au Palazzo della Rovere. Ces pièces datent du 10e siècle et viennent de différentes régions d'Angleterre. Avec elles, des objets artisanaux comme du cuir et du métal ont aussi été trouvés. C’est la première preuve matérielle que ce quartier anglais existait vraiment et que leurs pièces étaient utilisées.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle montre que les Anglais à Rome pouvaient utiliser leur propre monnaie, ce qui était rare à cette époque. En général, seules les monnaies locales étaient acceptées. Ce trésor donne aussi des détails sur la vie dans ce quartier, prouvant qu’il était actif et spécial dans la ville.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à étudier ces pièces et objets pour mieux comprendre comment vivait cette communauté anglaise à Rome. Ils veulent savoir comment les Anglais interagissaient avec les autorités papales et comment ce statut particulier influençait le commerce et la vie quotidienne.

**Phrase clé** – Un trésor rare de pièces anglo-saxonnes à Rome confirme que les résidents anglais du Moyen Âge jouissaient de privilèges uniques et formaient une communauté dynamique au cœur de la ville papale.
articles.personality_title_es: Monedas medievales inglesas revelan estatus especial en Roma
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los historiadores sabían por escritos antiguos que los ingleses vivían en un barrio llamado Schola Saxonum en la Roma medieval. Este lugar era un espacio donde viajeros y residentes ingleses tenían derechos especiales.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente se encontró un pequeño tesoro de monedas inglesas medievales cerca del Vaticano, en el Palazzo della Rovere. Estas monedas datan del siglo X y provienen de diferentes regiones de Inglaterra. Junto a ellas, también se hallaron restos de artesanías como cuero y metal. Esta es la primera prueba física que confirma que el barrio inglés realmente existió y que sus monedas se usaban.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque muestra que los ingleses en Roma podían usar su propia moneda, algo raro en esa época. Normalmente, solo se aceptaban monedas locales. El hallazgo también da detalles sobre la vida en el barrio, demostrando que era un lugar activo y especial dentro de la ciudad.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando las monedas y objetos para entender mejor cómo vivía esta comunidad inglesa en Roma. Quieren saber cómo interactuaban con las autoridades papales y cómo este estatus especial afectaba el comercio y la vida diaria.

**Frase clave** – Un raro tesoro de monedas anglosajonas en Roma confirma que los residentes ingleses medievales tenían privilegios únicos y formaban una comunidad vibrante en el corazón de la ciudad papal.
